claim: The mammalian cochlea loses its ability to regenerate new hair cells prior to the onset of hearing.
source: The mammalian cochlea loses its ability to regenerate new hair cells prior to the onset of hearing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about cochlear development.

claim: The adult vestibular system can produce new hair cells in response to damage.
source: In contrast, the adult vestibular system can produce new hair cells in response to damage, or by reprogramming of supporting cells with the hair cell transcription factor Atoh1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The adult vestibular system can produce new hair cells by reprogramming of supporting cells with the hair cell transcription factor Atoh1.
source: In contrast, the adult vestibular system can produce new hair cells in response to damage, or by reprogramming of supporting cells with the hair cell transcription factor Atoh1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experiments in the manuscript.

claim: The regenerative response of the utricle correlates with a more accessible chromatin structure in utricle supporting cells compared to their cochlear counterparts.
source: We show that the regenerative response of the utricle correlates with a more accessible chromatin structure in utricle supporting cells compared to their cochlear counterparts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by ATAC-seq data presented in the results.

claim: Atoh1 transduction of supporting cells is able to promote increased transcriptional accessibility of some hair cell genes.
source: We also provide evidence that Atoh1 transduction of supporting cells is able to promote increased transcriptional accessibility of some hair cell genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ATAC-seq data comparing Atoh1-transduced and control cells.

claim: Additional factors to Atoh1 may be required for optimal reprogramming of hair cell fate.
source: Our study offers a possible explanation for regenerative differences between sensory organs of the inner ear, but shows that additional factors to Atoh1 may be required for optimal reprogramming of hair cell fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Atoh1 alone does not fully reprogram supporting cells to hair cells.

claim: Sensory hair cells are exquisitely sensitive mechanosensors present in the inner ear and lateral line organs of vertebrates.
source: Sensory hair cells are exquisitely sensitive mechanosensors present in the inner ear and lateral line organs of vertebrates.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about hair cells.

claim: Hair cells are extremely vulnerable to the mechanical trauma of environmental noise exposure.
source: They are extremely vulnerable to the mechanical trauma of environmental noise exposure, and to ototoxic aminoglycoside antibiotics and platinum-containing chemotherapeutics (Oesterle, 2013; Liberman, 2016; Francis and Cunningham, 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Liberman, 2017; Sheth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Hair cells are extremely vulnerable to ototoxic aminoglycoside antibiotics and platinum-containing chemotherapeutics.
source: They are extremely vulnerable to the mechanical trauma of environmental noise exposure, and to ototoxic aminoglycoside antibiotics and platinum-containing chemotherapeutics (Oesterle, 2013; Liberman, 2016; Francis and Cunningham, 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Liberman, 2017; Sheth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Non-mammalian vertebrates are able to regenerate significant numbers of hair cells and achieve impressive functional recovery following deafening.
source: Non-mammalian vertebrates are able to regenerate significant numbers of hair cells and achieve impressive functional recovery following deafening (Brignull et al., 2009; Ryals et al., 2013; Monroe et al., 2015), and naturally replenish hair cells in their vestibular and lateral line sensory organs by an ongoing process of self-renewal (Corwin, 1981; Corwin, 1985; Jørgensen and Mathiesen, 1988; Roberson et al., 1992; Kil et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on non-mammalian vertebrates.

claim: Non-mammalian vertebrates naturally replenish hair cells in their vestibular and lateral line sensory organs by an ongoing process of self-renewal.
source: Non-mammalian vertebrates are able to regenerate significant numbers of hair cells and achieve impressive functional recovery following deafening (Brignull et al., 2009; Ryals et al., 2013; Monroe et al., 2015), and naturally replenish hair cells in their vestibular and lateral line sensory organs by an ongoing process of self-renewal (Corwin, 1981; Corwin, 1985; Jørgensen and Mathiesen, 1988; Roberson et al., 1992; Kil et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Regenerative processes in non-mammalian vertebrates involve the mobilization of neighboring supporting cells to re-enter the cell cycle and trans-differentiate into hair cells.
source: These regenerative processes involve the mobilization of neighboring supporting cells to re-enter the cell cycle and trans-differentiate into hair cells (Cotanche, 1987; Corwin and Cotanche, 1988; Ryals and Rubel, 1988; Stone and Cotanche, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on regeneration mechanisms.

claim: The mammalian hearing organ, the organ of Corti, has an extremely limited capacity for spontaneous regeneration.
source: In contrast, the mammalian hearing organ, the organ of Corti, has an extremely limited capacity for spontaneous regeneration, and this has only been observed in immature or embryonic mammals (Kelley et al., 1995; Bramhall et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2014; Atkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on mammalian cochlear regeneration.

claim: Spontaneous regeneration in the mammalian organ of Corti has only been observed in immature or embryonic mammals.
source: In contrast, the mammalian hearing organ, the organ of Corti, has an extremely limited capacity for spontaneous regeneration, and this has only been observed in immature or embryonic mammals (Kelley et al., 1995; Bramhall et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2014; Atkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A variety of manipulations can induce neonatal supporting cells to divide and trans-differentiate into hair cell-like cells in immature mice and rats.
source: A variety of manipulations, performed mostly in immature mice and rats, can induce neonatal supporting cells to divide and trans-differentiate into hair cell-like cells (Atkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Placing supporting cells in dissociated cell culture can induce them to divide and trans-differentiate into hair cell-like cells.
source: These include placing supporting cells in dissociated cell culture (White et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Sinkkonen et al., 2011), inhibition of the Notch signaling pathway, and activation of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway (Shi et al., 2013; Atkinson et al., 2015; Kuo et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015; Zak et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2016; Maass et al., 2016; Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inhibition of the Notch signaling pathway can induce neonatal supporting cells to divide and trans-differentiate into hair cell-like cells.
source: These include placing supporting cells in dissociated cell culture (White et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Sinkkonen et al., 2011), inhibition of the Notch signaling pathway, and activation of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway (Shi et al., 2013; Atkinson et al., 2015; Kuo et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015; Zak et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2016; Maass et al., 2016; Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activation of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway can induce neonatal supporting cells to divide and trans-differentiate into hair cell-like cells.
source: These include placing supporting cells in dissociated cell culture (White et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Sinkkonen et al., 2011), inhibition of the Notch signaling pathway, and activation of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway (Shi et al., 2013; Atkinson et al., 2015; Kuo et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015; Zak et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2016; Maass et al., 2016; Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Forced expression of the hair cell-specific transcription factor Atoh1 can cause supporting cells and non-sensory cells of the cochlea to convert to hair cell-like cells.
source: In addition, forced expression of the hair cell-specific transcription factor Atoh1 can cause supporting cells and non-sensory cells of the cochlea to convert to hair cell-like cells (Zheng and Gao, 2000; Kawamoto et al., 2003; Izumikawa et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012a; Yang et al., 2012b; Chen et al., 2013; Atkinson et al., 2014; Kuo et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The mammalian cochlea becomes refractory to regenerative manipulations as the organ of Corti matures.
source: However, the mammalian cochlea becomes refractory to these various manipulations as the organ of Corti matures, and almost no regeneration can be induced after the onset of hearing (Kelly et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Almost no regeneration can be induced in the cochlea after the onset of hearing.
source: However, the mammalian cochlea becomes refractory to these various manipulations as the organ of Corti matures, and almost no regeneration can be induced after the onset of hearing (Kelly et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Supporting cells are neither added nor replaced in the organ of Corti during the period when it becomes refractory to regeneration.
source: As supporting cells are neither added nor replaced in the organ of Corti during this period, it is likely that maturation of cochlear supporting cells is responsible for their failure to divide and differentiate into hair cells.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about cochlear development.

claim: Maturation of cochlear supporting cells is likely responsible for their failure to divide and differentiate into hair cells.
source: As supporting cells are neither added nor replaced in the organ of Corti during this period, it is likely that maturation of cochlear supporting cells is responsible for their failure to divide and differentiate into hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that supporting cells are not replaced during maturation.

claim: Mature mammalian vestibular organs are capable of a very limited, but significant, amount of ongoing hair cell production and regeneration following damage.
source: In contrast to the mammalian cochlea, mature mammalian vestibular organs are capable of a very limited, but significant, amount of ongoing hair cell production and regeneration following damage (Forge et al., 1993; Rubel et al., 1995; Kuntz and Oesterle, 1998; Ogata et al., 1999; Kawamoto et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2011; Golub et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Small numbers of immature hair cells have been observed in the adult mammalian utricle, including in humans.
source: Small numbers of immature hair cells have been observed in the adult mammalian utricle, including in humans (Taylor et al., 2015), and recent use of lineage tracing techniques have clearly demonstrated that small numbers of supporting cells can trans-differentiate into cells resembling type II hair cells in the adult mouse utricle, at a rate of about two hair cells added per week (Bucks et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Small numbers of supporting cells can trans-differentiate into cells resembling type II hair cells in the adult mouse utricle, at a rate of about two hair cells added per week.
source: Small numbers of immature hair cells have been observed in the adult mammalian utricle, including in humans (Taylor et al., 2015), and recent use of lineage tracing techniques have clearly demonstrated that small numbers of supporting cells can trans-differentiate into cells resembling type II hair cells in the adult mouse utricle, at a rate of about two hair cells added per week (Bucks et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research using lineage tracing.

claim: The rate of hair cell replacement in the adult utricle increases significantly after hair cells are experimentally killed.
source: This rate of replacement increases significantly after hair cells are experimentally killed (Bucks et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hair cell production in the adult utricle involves up-regulation of the Atoh1 transcription factor.
source: Hair cell production in the adult utricle is superficially similar to that observed during embryonic hair cell formation in mammals: it involves up-regulation of the Atoh1 transcription factor, and is regulated by the Notch signaling pathway (Wang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2011; Golub et al., 2012; Bucks et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hair cell production in the adult utricle is regulated by the Notch signaling pathway.
source: Hair cell production in the adult utricle is superficially similar to that observed during embryonic hair cell formation in mammals: it involves up-regulation of the Atoh1 transcription factor, and is regulated by the Notch signaling pathway (Wang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2011; Golub et al., 2012; Bucks et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Overexpression of the Atoh1 transcription factor in normal or ototoxin-treated adult utricle organ cultures leads to a robust production of hair cell-like cells.
source: Indeed, overexpression of the Atoh1 transcription factor in normal or ototoxin-treated adult utricle organ cultures or immature mice leads to a robust production of hair cell-like cells (Shou et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Overexpression of the Atoh1 transcription factor in immature mice leads to a robust production of hair cell-like cells.
source: Indeed, overexpression of the Atoh1 transcription factor in normal or ototoxin-treated adult utricle organ cultures or immature mice leads to a robust production of hair cell-like cells (Shou et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Approximately 80% of utricle hair cells were labeled by tamoxifen delivery from P10 to P14 in Atoh1-CreERT2; Ai3 mice.
source: Three weeks later, we dissected the labeled utricles and used antibodies to GFP and Myosin7a to show that approximately 80% of utricle hair cells were labeled by this approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The purified hair cell population contained fewer than 1% supporting cells.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of the purified hair cell population with markers of supporting cells showed they contained fewer than 1% supporting cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: CD326, a 40 kDa mouse EpCAM glycoprotein, is expressed by both utricle hair cells and supporting cells but not underlying stromal cells.
source: To isolate utricle supporting cells, we made use of the fact that CD326, a 40 kDa mouse EpCAM glycoprotein is expressed by both utricle hair cells and supporting cells but not underlying stromal cells (Hertzano et al., 2011; Sinkkonen et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The purified supporting cell population showed a complete absence of EYFP+ hair cells.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of the purified supporting cell population showed a complete absence of EYFP +hair cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claim: 1912 transcripts were more than four-fold enriched in utricle hair cells.
source: Following RNA-seq analysis of the purified utricle hair cells and supporting cells, we performed differential expression analysis and identified 1912 transcripts more than four-fold enriched in utricle hair cells and 2619 transcripts more than four-fold enriched in supporting cells (adj. p<0.05; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 2619 transcripts were more than four-fold enriched in utricle supporting cells.
source: Following RNA-seq analysis of the purified utricle hair cells and supporting cells, we performed differential expression analysis and identified 1912 transcripts more than four-fold enriched in utricle hair cells and 2619 transcripts more than four-fold enriched in supporting cells (adj. p<0.05; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 70 of the top 100 enriched utricle hair cell genes have been previously reported in transcriptomic or proteomic studies of hair cells.
source: 70 of the top 100 enriched utricle hair cell genes have been previously reported in transcriptomic or proteomic studies of hair cells (Cai et al., 2015; Scheffer et al., 2015; Hickox et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a validation of the RNA-seq data by comparison with previous studies.

claim: 47 of the top 100 supporting cell-enriched genes have previously been shown to be expressed in cochlear supporting cells.
source: Although the transcriptome of supporting cells has been less well-characterized than that of hair cells, of our top 100 supporting cell-enriched genes, 47 have previously been shown to be expressed in cochlear supporting cells (Maass et al., 2016 ; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a validation of the RNA-seq data by comparison with previous studies.

claim: Adenoviral serotype 5 (dE1) specifically infects adult utricle supporting cells.
source: We chose this serotype as previous studies showed it specifically infects adult utricle supporting cells (Brandon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Almost none of the infected cells expressed the hair cell marker Myo7a two days after infection with Ad-tdTomato.
source: Almost none of the infected cells expressed the hair cell marker Myo7a; out of two explants analyzed, we observed only a single tdTomato expressing cell co-expressing Myo7a protein, indicating our adenovirus specifically infects supporting cells in mature utricle explants.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data from the experiments.

claim: Five days after transduction with Ad-Atoh1-tdTomato virus, about 45% of infected supporting cells expressed Myo7a.
source: In cultures infected with Ad-Atoh1-tdTomato virus, we began to observe clear Myo7a staining in about 45% of infected supporting cells five days after transduction (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ten days after transduction with Ad-Atoh1-tdTomato virus, more than 80% of the infected cells expressed Myo7a.
source: Ten days after transduction with Ad-Atoh1-tdTomato virus, more than 80% of the infected cells expressed Myo7a (Figure 2E–G), while cells infected with Ad-tdTomato virus remained Myo7a negative ten days after infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Cells infected with Ad-tdTomato virus remained Myo7a negative ten days after infection.
source: Ten days after transduction with Ad-Atoh1-tdTomato virus, more than 80% of the infected cells expressed Myo7a (Figure 2E–G), while cells infected with Ad-tdTomato virus remained Myo7a negative ten days after infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 24 hr of exposure to gentamicin led to significant hair cell loss in the utricle in a dose-dependent manner.
source: 24 hr of exposure to gentamicin led to significant hair cell loss in the utricle in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and hair cell counts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Supporting cells from cultures treated with 1 mM gentamicin for 24 hr had an abnormal, elongated morphology after 5 days.
source: We observed that supporting cells from cultures treated with 1 mM gentamicin for 24 hr had an abnormal, elongated morphology after 5 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cultures treated with 0.1 mM gentamicin for 24 hr had lost significant numbers of hair cells after 5 days, but the remaining supporting cells retained a normal morphology.
source: In contrast, cultures treated with 0.1 mM gentamicin for 24 hr had lost significant numbers of hair cells after 5 days, but the remaining supporting cells retained a normal morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with 0.1 mM gentamicin initiated apoptosis within 24 hr.
source: Treatment with 0.1 mM gentamicin initiated apoptosis within 24 hr, measured by incubation with Caspase-3 enzyme substrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C; Cunningham et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by Caspase-3 activity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Ad-tdTomato infected cells occupied an intermediate transcriptional space between utricle hair cells and supporting cells.
source: As expected, principal component analysis showed that Ad-tdTomato infected cells occupied an intermediate transcriptional space between utricle hair cells and supporting cells, and that Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 infected cells more closely resembled endogenous utricle hair cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 infected cells more closely resembled endogenous utricle hair cells than Ad-tdTomato infected cells.
source: As expected, principal component analysis showed that Ad-tdTomato infected cells occupied an intermediate transcriptional space between utricle hair cells and supporting cells, and that Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 infected cells more closely resembled endogenous utricle hair cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ad-tdTomato-infected supporting cells up-regulated 599 hair cell transcripts after a brief treatment with gentamicin followed by culture for 10 days.
source: We found that Ad-tdTomato-infected supporting cells up-regulated significant numbers of hair cell genes after a brief treatment with gentamicin followed by culture for 10 days (Figure 3B). We identified 599 hair cell transcripts that were up-regulated after this treatment.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Transduction of utricle cultures with Atoh1 induced an additional 346 hair cell genes beyond those induced by damage alone.
source: However, transduction of utricle cultures with Atoh1 induced an additional 346 hair cell genes (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and analysis shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: 112 of the 346 additional hair cell genes induced by Atoh1 are also expressed in neonatal cochlear hair cells.
source: 112 of these genes appear to be generic markers of hair cells, as they are also expressed in neonatal cochlear hair cells (Cai et al., 2015; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published neonatal cochlear hair cell data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 967 out of 1912 utricle hair cell genes were not significantly up-regulated in utricle supporting cells after damage and Atoh1 transduction.
source: Although many hair cell genes were up-regulated in supporting cells after damage and Atoh1 transduction, many other utricle hair cell genes (967 out of 1912 genes) were not significantly up-regulated in utricle supporting cells in either of these conditions (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and analysis shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Many hair cell genes that were not up-regulated by damage or Atoh1 transduction were associated with maturation or function of hair cells.
source: We performed GO analysis for these hair cell genes and found significant numbers of genes associated with maturation or function of hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: Infection of supporting cells with Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 virus up-regulated 440 genes that were neither present in mature hair cells, nor up-regulated by hair cell damage and culture alone.
source: We also observed that infection of supporting cells with Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 virus up-regulated a significant number of genes (440 genes) that were neither present in mature hair cells, nor up-regulated by hair cell damage and culture alone (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Atoh1 transduction is unlikely to be specifically up-regulating Atoh1 gene regulatory networks that normally function in other Atoh1-expressing cell types.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that Atoh1 transduction is specifically up-regulating Atoh1 gene regulatory networks that normally function in other Atoh1-expressing cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of genes induced by Atoh1 in supporting cells compared to genes expressed in other Atoh1-expressing tissues.

claim: 608 supporting cell genes were significantly down-regulated in utricle supporting cells after hair cell killing and culture.
source: Several hundred supporting cell genes (608 were significantly down regulated in utricle supporting cells after hair cell killing and culture (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), including some genes associated with differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 107 additional supporting cell genes were down-regulated when utricle supporting cells were infected with Atoh1 virus.
source: A small number (107) of additional supporting cell genes were down-regulated when utricle supporting cells were infected with Atoh1 virus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Many supporting cell genes remained expressed in cultured utricles after 10 days.
source: Significantly, many supporting cell genes remained expressed in our cultured utricles after 10 days.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing persistent expression of supporting cell genes.

claim: tdTomato-Atoh1 and tdTomato transduced supporting cells tended to cluster separately in hierarchical clustering analysis based on expression of the top 500 hair cell-specific genes.
source: Although we observed a heterogeneity in the relative expression of hair cell genes across individual cells, tdTomato-Atoh1 and tdTomato transduced supporting cells tended to cluster separately.
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Many previously identified hair cell genes were expressed at higher levels in Atoh1-transduced cells compared with TdTomato alone.
source: Many previously identified hair cell genes were expressed at higher levels in Atoh1-transduced cells compared with TdTomato alone – for example Pou4f3, Gfi1, Tmc1, Lhx3, Pvalb, Tomt, Mgat5b, Mreg and Rab15 (Cai et al., 2015; Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A subset of hair cell genes did not show significant differences between Atoh1- and tdTomato-transduced cells.
source: However, we also saw a subset of hair cell genes that did not show significant differences between Atoh1- and tdTomato-transduced cells (for example, Fscn2; Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Supporting cells that were transduced with Atoh1 tended to express lower levels of the top 500 supporting cell genes compared to supporting cells that received tdTomato virus alone.
source: As expected, supporting cells that were transduced with Atoh1 tended to express lower levels of the top 500 supporting cell genes compared to supporting cells that received tdTomato virus alone.
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adult utricle supporting cells maintain some hair cell loci in a transcriptionally accessible state.
source: However, we also observed the presence of accessible DNA, indicative of relatively open chromatin, around the transcriptional start sites, intergenic regions and introns of hair cell gene loci in utricle supporting cells (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting that adult utricle supporting cells maintain some hair cell loci in a transcriptionally accessible state.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Hair cell loci that are accessible in utricle supporting cells are expressed at 1–2 orders of magnitude lower levels in supporting cells than hair cells.
source: However, these hair cell loci were nevertheless expressed at 1–2 orders of magnitude lower levels in supporting cells than hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data.

claim: There was no correlation between the expression levels of hair cell genes in cochlear supporting cells and their relative chromatin accessibility (r = 0.04).
source: Moreover, we saw no correlation between the expression levels of hair cell genes in either cochlear (r = 0.04) or utricle (r = 0.02) supporting cells and their relative chromatin accessibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There was no correlation between the expression levels of hair cell genes in utricle supporting cells and their relative chromatin accessibility (r = 0.02).
source: Moreover, we saw no correlation between the expression levels of hair cell genes in either cochlear (r = 0.04) or utricle (r = 0.02) supporting cells and their relative chromatin accessibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Peaks that were accessible in mature utricle hair cells and supporting cells were comparatively less accessible in mature cochlear supporting cells at distal enhancer regions.
source: However, when we analyzed ATAC-seq peaks in distal regions more typically associated with enhancers, we saw that peaks that were accessible in mature utricle hair cells and supporting cells were comparatively less accessible in mature cochlear supporting cells (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Differential chromatin accessibility may be one explanation for why mature cochlear supporting cells may not undergo spontaneous regeneration or trans-differentiation after expression of Atoh1.
source: This suggests that differential chromatin accessibility may be one explanation for why mature cochlear supporting cells may not undergo spontaneous regeneration or trans-differentiation after expression of Atoh1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATAC-seq data showing differences in chromatin accessibility between utricle and cochlear supporting cells.

claim: There were no significant differences in chromatin accessibility in supporting cells around the TSS, intergenic regions or introns for the 945 up-regulated hair cell genes compared to the 967 hair cell genes that were not up-regulated.
source: We observed no significant differences in chromatin accessibility in supporting cells around the TSS, intergenic regions or introns for the 945 up-regulated hair cell genes compared to the 967 hair cell genes that were not up-regulated (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Relative chromatin accessibility is not likely to be a significant determinant of whether a hair cell gene can be activated in utricle supporting cells after cell death or Atoh1 transduction.
source: These data suggest that relative chromatin accessibility is not likely to be a significant determinant of whether a hair cell gene can be activated in utricle supporting cells after cell death or Atoh1 transduction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATAC-seq data showing no correlation between accessibility and gene activation.

claim: Transduction of supporting cells with Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 can render some hair cell gene regions accessible to a comparable degree to hair cells.
source: However, transduction of supporting cells with Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 but not Ad-tdTomato renders this region accessible to a comparable degree to hair cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6B for the Rasd2 gene.

claim: Atoh1 binding motifs were enriched in the open regions of Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 infected cells (P value = 1.00E-107).
source: We observed that Atoh1 binding motifs were enriched in the open regions of Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 infected cells (P value = 1.00E-107; Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; Figure 6—source data 1), but not in Ad-tdTomato infected cells (p value = 1; Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by de novo motif analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Atoh1 binding motifs were not enriched in the open regions of Ad-tdTomato infected cells (p value = 1).
source: We observed that Atoh1 binding motifs were enriched in the open regions of Ad-tdTomato-Atoh1 infected cells (P value = 1.00E-107; Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; Figure 6—source data 1), but not in Ad-tdTomato infected cells (p value = 1; Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by de novo motif analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Activation of Atoh1 in supporting cells can either directly or indirectly reprogram the epigenetic landscape of utricle supporting cells to make some hair cell genes loci more accessible.
source: Together, these results suggest that activation of Atoh1 in supporting cells can either directly or indirectly reprogram the epigenetic landscape of utricle supporting cells to make some hair cell genes loci more accessible.
evidence: This is an inference based on ATAC-seq data showing changes in chromatin accessibility after Atoh1 transduction.

claim: Increased chromatin accessibility around a given gene does not necessarily imply that gene will be transcribed.
source: However, increased chromatin accessibility around a given gene does not necessarily imply that gene will be transcribed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the example of Kcnj13 shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Atoh1 is able to cause opening of the chromatin around some hair cell gene loci, but this opening does not necessarily lead to transcription of those genes.
source: This shows that Atoh1 is able to cause opening of the chromatin around some hair cell gene loci, but that this opening does not necessarily lead to transcription of those genes, suggesting additional transcription factors may be required to activate transcription of a given gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data showing chromatin opening without gene activation.

claim: Atoh1 transduction leads to the opening of several hundred peaks that are not present in utricle hair cells.
source: Furthermore, we observed that Atoh1 transduction also leads to the opening of several hundred peaks that are not present in utricle hair cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: Some of the genes induced by Atoh1 may be activated by Atoh1 engaging cryptic binding sites.
source: This raises the possibility that some of the genes induced by Atoh1 may be activated by Atoh1 engaging cryptic binding sites.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Atoh1 opens chromatin regions not present in hair cells.

claim: Vestibular supporting cells in the adult mouse undergo a very slow rate of hair cell turnover.
source: Vestibular supporting cells in the adult mouse undergo a very slow rate of hair cell turnover (Bucks et al., 2017) and do not show a significant response to Atoh1 transduction (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Vestibular supporting cells in the adult mouse do not show a significant response to Atoh1 transduction.
source: Vestibular supporting cells in the adult mouse undergo a very slow rate of hair cell turnover (Bucks et al., 2017) and do not show a significant response to Atoh1 transduction (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hair cell killing by aminoglycosides, extended cell culture or genetic ablation strategies appears to prime adult vestibular supporting cells to up-regulate some hair cell genes and generate hair cell-like cells.
source: In contrast, hair cell killing by aminoglycosides, extended cell culture or genetic ablation strategies appears to prime adult vestibular supporting cells to up-regulate some hair cell genes and generate hair cell-like cells (Golub et al., 2012; Bucks et al., 2017), and this hair cell generation can be enhanced by interventions such as Atoh1 transduction or Notch inhibition (Shou et al., 2003; Golub et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hair cell generation in the adult vestibular system can be enhanced by interventions such as Atoh1 transduction or Notch inhibition.
source: In contrast, hair cell killing by aminoglycosides, extended cell culture or genetic ablation strategies appears to prime adult vestibular supporting cells to up-regulate some hair cell genes and generate hair cell-like cells (Golub et al., 2012; Bucks et al., 2017), and this hair cell generation can be enhanced by interventions such as Atoh1 transduction or Notch inhibition (Shou et al., 2003; Golub et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Significant transcriptional changes occur in utricle supporting cells over a ten day period after hair cell damage.
source: Consistent with the idea that hair cell damage allows supporting cells to adopt a cell state that is more amenable to trans-differentiation into hair cells, we observed significant transcriptional changes in utricle supporting cells over a ten day period.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data from the experiments.

claim: Supporting cells that undergo transcriptional changes after hair cell damage do not display any overt morphological features of hair cells.
source: However, these cells did not display any overt morphological features of hair cells, nor did they up-regulate canonical markers of hair cells such as Myosin7a.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data from the experiments.

claim: Supporting cells that undergo transcriptional changes after hair cell damage do not up-regulate canonical markers of hair cells such as Myosin7a.
source: However, these cells did not display any overt morphological features of hair cells, nor did they up-regulate canonical markers of hair cells such as Myosin7a.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and RNA-seq data from the experiments.

claim: Adenoviral transduction of Atoh1 was required to induce expression of hundreds of additional hair cell genes beyond those induced by damage alone.
source: Adenoviral transduction of Atoh1 was required to induce expression of hundreds of additional hair cell genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The chromatin around the loci of hair cell genes common to the cochlea and utricle is more accessible in utricle supporting cells compared to their cochlear counterparts.
source: Our ATAC-seq experiments show that the chromatin around the loci of hair cell genes common to the cochlea and utricle is more accessible in utricle supporting cells compared to their cochlear counterparts, which may underlie their higher capacity for regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data comparing utricle and cochlear supporting cells.

claim: Genes involved in histone remodeling are important regulators of supporting cell proliferation in chicken and zebrafish.
source: Studies in chicken and zebrafish, which exhibit spontaneous hair cell regeneration, have demonstrated that genes involved in histone remodeling are important regulators of supporting cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by the discussion of previous research on histone remodeling in regenerating systems.

claim: HDAC inhibition in regenerating vestibular epithelium results in decreased supporting cell proliferation in birds.
source: In birds, HDAC inhibition in regenerating vestibular epithelium results in decreased supporting cell proliferation (Slattery et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HDAC inhibition results in reduced lateral line supporting cell proliferation and hair cell regeneration in zebrafish.
source: Similarly in zebrafish, HDAC inhibition result in reduced lateral line supporting cell proliferation and thus hair cell regeneration (He et al., 2014; He et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inhibition of lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1, also known as KDM1A) in zebrafish prevents supporting cell proliferation.
source: Inhibition of lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1, also known as KDM1A) in zebrafish also prevents supporting cell proliferation (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: BMI1, part of the Polycomb repressive complex1 (PRC1), is required for supporting cell proliferation in neonatal mice by maintaining high levels of canonical Wnt signaling.
source: Finally, a recent study showed that BMI1, part of the Polycomb repressive complex1 (PRC1), is required for supporting cell proliferation in neonatal mice by maintaining high levels of canonical Wnt signaling (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Almost 1000 utricle hair cell genes were not up-regulated in supporting cells, even after hair cell killing and Atoh1 transduction.
source: Despite the large number of hair cell genes that could be activated in mature utricle supporting cells, we nevertheless observed almost 1000 utricle hair cell genes that were not up-regulated in supporting cells, even after hair cell killing and Atoh1 transduction.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data from the experiments.

claim: Many hair cell genes that were not up-regulated by damage and Atoh1 transduction were associated with maturation of hair cell function, including hair bundle and kinocilium development.
source: Many of these genes were associated with maturation of hair cell function, including hair bundle and kinocilium development.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: A recent study in which human utricle tissue was transduced with an Atoh1 adenovirus reported phenotypes consistent with incomplete hair cell differentiation.
source: A recent study in which human utricle tissue was transduced with an Atoh1 adenovirus also reported phenotypes consistent with incomplete hair cell differentiation, including an absence of stereocilia and actin bundling proteins such as espin, and an absence of a cuticular plate and ribbon synapses (Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Studies of cellular reprogramming by transcription factors suggest that reprogramming events at the level of single cells initially proceed in a stochastic manner before an eventual entrainment of the fully reprogrammed state.
source: Studies of cellular reprogramming by transcription factors suggest that reprogramming events at the level of single cells initially proceed in a stochastic manner before an eventual entrainment of the fully reprogrammed state (Hanna et al., 2009; Buganim et al., 2012; Lujan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on cellular reprogramming.

claim: Single cell analysis shows a wide degree of heterogeneity in transcriptional responses to Atoh1 transduction.
source: Our single cell analysis (Figure 4), together with a recent single cell analysis of Atoh1 activation in the cochlea (Yamashita et al., 2018), show a wide degree of heterogeneity in transcriptional responses to Atoh1 transduction that may underlie this incomplete transformation to hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4 and a citation to previous research.

claim: Atoh1 is normally down-regulated as hair cells differentiate.
source: Alternatively, since Atoh1 is normally down-regulated as hair cells differentiate (Shailam et al., 1999; Driver et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015), it is possible that persistent expression of Atoh1 after adenoviral infection actively represses genes associated with hair cell maturation that would normally be activated as Atoh1 levels decline.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Persistent expression of Atoh1 after adenoviral infection may actively repress genes associated with hair cell maturation that would normally be activated as Atoh1 levels decline.
source: Alternatively, since Atoh1 is normally down-regulated as hair cells differentiate (Shailam et al., 1999; Driver et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015), it is possible that persistent expression of Atoh1 after adenoviral infection actively represses genes associated with hair cell maturation that would normally be activated as Atoh1 levels decline.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism for incomplete reprogramming.

claim: Some hair cell genes may be regulated entirely independently of Atoh1 and are unaffected by Atoh1 expression.
source: A third possibility is that some hair cell genes are regulated entirely independently of Atoh1 and are unaffected by Atoh1 expression.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism for incomplete reprogramming.

claim: Some hair cell genes may require additional transcription factors or co-activators for expression (for example, Gfi1 and Pou4f3).
source: Alternatively, some hair cell genes may require additional transcription factors or co-activators for expression (for example, Gfi1 and Pou4f3; Costa and Henrique, 2015; Costa et al., 2015), and these are not up-regulated by Atoh1 expression alone.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous research on hair cell transcription factors.

claim: Many supporting cell genes remained expressed in utricle supporting cells despite 10 days of culture and Atoh1 expression.
source: When we examined the behavior of supporting cell genes in response to hair cell killing and Atoh1 transduction, we also found many genes that remained expressed in utricle supporting cells despite 10 days of culture and Atoh1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data from the experiments.

claim: Chromatin accessibility is not a good predictor of whether a hair cell gene is induced by Atoh1 in utricle supporting cells.
source: Our data thus suggest that chromatin accessibility is not a good predictor of whether a hair cell gene is induced by Atoh1 in utricle supporting cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data showing no correlation between accessibility and gene induction.

claim: While Atoh1 may be sufficient to induce the expression of some hair cell genes, additional transcription factors or chromatin remodelers may be necessary to induce a full complement of hair cell genes in supporting cells.
source: Rather, we suggest that while Atoh1 may be sufficient to induce the expression of some hair cell genes, additional transcription factors or chromatin remodelers may be necessary to induce a full complement of hair cell genes in supporting cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Atoh1 alone does not induce all hair cell genes.

claim: A number of transcription factors have been proposed to co-operate with Atoh1 during hair cell induction, such as Gfi1, Pou4f3, Isl1, Gata3 and targets of the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: A number of transcription factors have been proposed to co-operate with Atoh1 during hair cell induction, such as Gfi1, Pou4f3, Isl1, Gata3 and targets of the Wnt signaling pathway (Costa and Henrique, 2015; Costa et al., 2015; Kuo et al., 2015; Walters et al., 2017; Yamashita et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on hair cell transcription factors.

claim: Systematic combinatorial testing of transcription factors in the context of a better defined hair cell gene regulatory network will be required to define the best cocktail of hair cell transcription factors required for optimum reprogramming of a hair cell fate.
source: Systematic combinatorial testing of these transcription factors in the context of a better defined hair cell gene regulatory network will be required to define the best cocktail of hair cell transcription factors required for optimum reprogramming of a hair cell fate.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the findings of the study.
